summary_html: The **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** created a national commission to study child-fatality prevention. Project Milk Carton cross-references its findings with state fatality data to expose non-implementation.
authority_html: - **Public Law 112-275 (Protect Our Kids Act)** — national commission and reporting framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a state to protect a child from private violence, so a county's failure to remove a child it knew was being abused by his father did not violate substantive due process.
key_cases.relevance: Is the reason fatality review commissions exist: the Constitution supplies no remedy for most agency failures to protect.
key_cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

key_cases.case_name: B.H. v. County of San Bernardino
key_cases.holding: The court held that a law enforcement agency's CANRA duty to cross-report a child abuse report it receives to the county child welfare agency is a mandatory duty enforceable under Government Code section 815.6, distinct from the responding officer's separate investigative duties.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the private enforcement mechanism available when a fatality review traces the death to an agency's failure to perform a mandatory reporting duty.
key_cases.quote: These provisions indicate that a law enforcement agency's duty to cross-report the receipt of an initial child abuse or neglect report is separate from its investigative duties.

key_cases.case_name: Jacob B. v. County of Shasta
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Civil Code section 47(b) litigation privilege barred a damages action based on a county's disclosure of confidential juvenile record information in a letter filed in a family law proceeding, and that the privilege applies even to a claim grounded in the state constitutional right of privacy.
key_cases.relevance: Bears on who may obtain confidential juvenile records when reviewing an agency's handling of a case.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the litigation privilege applies even to a constitutionally based privacy cause of action.
